# Context-Rich Solid Mechanics Problem

## Motor-Driven Shaft Design for a Belt-Transmission System

### Engineering Context

Industrial facilities commonly use electric motors and belt-drive systems to transmit mechanical power to rotating equipment such as conveyors, pumps, fans, mixers, and production machinery. In a typical installation, the motor rotates a steel drive shaft carrying a pulley. The pulley transfers power through one or more belts to the driven machine. Bearings support the rotating shaft and maintain alignment while allowing the shaft to rotate freely.

The shaft is a critical load-carrying component because all mechanical power delivered from the motor to the pulley must pass through it as torque. For a given transmitted power, the required torque depends on rotational speed: lower-speed drives must transmit more torque than higher-speed drives carrying the same power. The shaft diameter therefore has a direct influence on the torsional shear stress and on whether the drive can safely transmit the required power.

In industrial design, shafts are commonly selected from available standard stock sizes rather than manufactured to an arbitrary theoretical diameter. The engineering task is therefore to determine the minimum diameter required by the allowable torsional shear stress and then select and verify an appropriate standard shaft size.

The base MEEN 305 analysis isolates steady torsion in the solid circular shaft. The real belt drive can also produce radial bearing reactions, shaft bending from belt tension, stress concentrations at keyways or shoulders, startup and shock torque, and fatigue under repeated service. Those effects are intentionally excluded here so that power, speed, torque, torsional shear stress, and shaft diameter remain the primary mechanics objective.

![Industrial motor, steel shaft, pulley, belts, and bearing support.](assets/shaft-industry-context.png){fig-alt="Industrial electric motor driving a belt pulley through a supported steel shaft." width=88%}

### Main Engineering Goal

Determine the minimum safe diameter of the solid steel drive shaft for the specified motor power and operating speed, select the next appropriate standard shaft size, and verify that the selected shaft does not exceed the specified allowable torsional shear stress.

### System Components

- electric motor;
- solid steel drive shaft;
- pulley and belt drive;
- bearing support;
- driven equipment.
